content: **Alfa Romeo Automobiles S.p.A.** (Italian:[[ˈalfaroˈmɛːo]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Italian)) is an Italian [car manufacturer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Car_manufacturer) known for its [sports-oriented](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_car) vehicles, strong [auto racing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auto_racing) heritage, and iconic design.[3] Headquartered in [Turin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turin), Italy, it is a [subsidiary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subsidiary) of [Stellantis Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stellantis_Europe) and one of 14 brands of [multinational](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multinational_corporation) automotive company [Stellantis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stellantis).

Founded on 24 June 1910 in [Milan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milan), Italy as **A.L.F.A.**—an acronym for *Anonima Lombarda Fabbrica Automobili*[a]—the company was established by Cavaliere Ugo Stella to acquire the assets of the ailing Italian subsidiary of French carmaker [Darracq](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Automobiles_Darracq_France), of which he had been an investor and manager.[4] Its first car was the [24 HP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ALFA_24_HP), designed by [Giuseppe Merosi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giuseppe_Merosi), which became commercially successful and participated in the 1911 [Targa Florio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Targa_Florio) endurance race.

In August 1915, ALFA was acquired by [Neapolitan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naples) entrepreneur and engineer [Nicola Romeo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicola_Romeo), who vastly expanded the company's portfolio to include heavy machinery and aircraft engines. In 1920, the company's name was changed to **Alfa Romeo**, with the [Torpedo 20–30 HP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfa_Romeo_20/30_HP) being the first vehicle to bear the new brand.

Through the 1920s, Alfa Romeo produced several successful road and race cars, and was well represented in prominent European motorsport events, notably winning the inaugural [AIACR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fédération_Internationale_de_l'Automobile) [World Manufacturers' Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Manufacturers'_Championship) at the [1925 Grand Prix season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1925_Grand_Prix_season). Nevertheless, the company soon faced financial troubles, leading to Romeo's contentious departure in 1928 and Italian government ownership in 1933.

Under the control of the industrial organization [*Institute for Industrial Reconstruction*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Istituto_per_la_Ricostruzione_Industriale) (IRI), Alfa Romeo initially continued making its signature custom luxury vehicles, but following the financial hardship of World War II, shifted to mass-producing small vehicles. In 1954, it launched the [Giulietta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfa_Romeo_Giulietta_(750/101)) series of [family cars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Family_car) and developed the [Alfa Romeo Twin Cam engine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfa_Romeo_Twin_Cam_engine), which would remain in production until 1994.

Alfa Romeo became known for producing mass-market vehicles that nonetheless blended the aesthetics and performance of sport and luxury marques. Despite its strong brand image and relatively sizeable share of the high-performance auto market in Europe, by the 1970s, the company was operating at a loss, prompting IRI to sell it to [Fiat Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fiat_Group) in 1986.[5]

Alfa Romeo has since maintained its distinct identity and brand through several ownership changes, including Fiat's merger with the American [Chrysler Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chrysler_Group) in 2014, forming [Fiat Chrysler Automobiles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fiat_Chrysler_Automobiles) (FCA), and FCA's subsequent merger in 2021 with the French [PSA Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PSA_Group) to form Stellantis.

Alfa Romeo is heavily [involved in various motorsports](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfa_Romeo_in_motorsport)—including [Grand Prix motor racing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Prix_motor_racing), [Formula One](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Formula_One), [sportscar racing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sportscar_racing), [touring car racing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Touring_car_racing), and [rallies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rallying)—with achievements giving a sporty image to the marque. [Enzo Ferrari](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enzo_Ferrari) founded the [Scuderia Ferrari](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scuderia_Ferrari) racing team in 1929 as an Alfa Romeo racing team, before forming [his namesake luxury sports car maker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferrari) in 1939.

content.heading: Name
content: The company's name is a combination of the original name, "A.L.F.A." ("Anonima Lombarda Fabbrica Automobili" - “Lombardian Automobile Factory Corporation”), and the last name of entrepreneur Nicola Romeo, who took control of the company in 1915.

content.heading: Foundation and early years
content: The first factory building of A.L.F.A. was in the first-place property of **Società Anonima Italiana Darracq** (SAID), founded in 1906 by the French automobile firm of [Alexandre Darracq](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexandre_Darracq), with some Italian investors. One of them, Cavaliere Ugo Stella, an aristocrat from [Milan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milan), became chairman of the SAID in 1909.[6] The firm's initial location was in [Naples](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naples), but even before the construction of the planned factory had started, Darracq decided late in 1906 that Milan would be more suitable and accordingly a tract of land was acquired in the Milan suburb of [Portello](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portello,_Milan), where a new factory of 6,700 square metres (8,000 sq yd) was constructed. In late 1909, the Italian Darracq cars were selling slowly and the company was wound up.[7] Ugo Stella, with the other Italian co-investors, founded a new company named **A.L.F.A.** (Anonima Lombarda Fabbrica Automobili), buying the assets of Italian Darracq that was up to dissolution.[7] The first car produced by the company was the 1910 [24 HP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ALFA_24_HP), designed by [Giuseppe Merosi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giuseppe_Merosi), hired in 1909 for designing new cars more suited to the Italian market. Merosi would go on to design a series of new A.L.F.A. cars, with more powerful engines such as the [40–60 HP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ALFA_40/60_HP). A.L.F.A. ventured into [motor racing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motor_racing), with drivers Franchini and Ronzoni competing in the 1911 [Targa Florio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Targa_Florio) with two 24-hp models. In 1914, an advanced Grand Prix car was designed and built, the [GP1914](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfa_Romeo_Grand_Prix), with a four-cylinder engine, double overhead camshafts, four valves per cylinder, and twin ignition.[8] However, the onset of the [First World War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_World_War) halted automobile production at A.L.F.A. for three years.

In August 1915, the company came under the direction of Neapolitan entrepreneur [Nicola Romeo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicola_Romeo), who converted the factory to produce military hardware for the Italian and Allied war efforts. Munitions, aircraft engines and other components, compressors, and generators based on the company's existing car engines were produced in a vastly enlarged factory during the war. After the war, Romeo invested his war profits in acquiring locomotive and railway carriage plants in Saronno ([Costruzioni Meccaniche di Saronno](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costruzioni_Meccaniche_di_Saronno)), Rome (Officine Meccaniche di Roma), and Naples (Officine Ferroviarie Meridionali), which were added to his A.L.F.A. ownership.

Car production had not been considered at first, but resumed in 1919 since parts for the completion of 105 cars had remained at the A.L.F.A. factory since 1915.[6] In 1920, the name of the company was changed to Alfa Romeo with the [Torpedo 20–30 HP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfa_Romeo_20/30_HP) the first car to be so badged.[10] Their first success came in 1920 when [Giuseppe Campari](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giuseppe_Campari) won at [Mugello](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mugello_Circuit) and continued with second place in the [Targa Florio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Targa_Florio) driven by [Enzo Ferrari](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enzo_Ferrari). Giuseppe Merosi continued as head designer, and the company continued to produce solid road cars as well as successful race cars (including the 40–60 HP and the [RL Targa Florio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfa_Romeo_RL)).

In 1923, [Vittorio Jano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vittorio_Jano) was lured from [Fiat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fiat), partly due to the persuasion of a young Alfa racing driver named Enzo Ferrari, to replace Merosi as chief designer at Alfa Romeo. The first Alfa Romeo under Jano was the [P2 Grand Prix car](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfa_Romeo_P2), which won Alfa Romeo the inaugural world championship for Grand Prix cars in 1925. For road cars, Jano developed a series of small-to-medium-displacement 4-, 6-, and 8-cylinder inline engines based on the P2 unit that established the architecture of the company's engines, with light alloy construction, [hemispherical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hemispherical_combustion_chamber) combustion chambers, centrally located plugs, two rows of overhead valves per cylinder bank and dual overhead cams. Jano's designs proved both reliable and powerful.

Enzo Ferrari proved a better team manager than a driver, and when the factory team was privatised, it became [Scuderia Ferrari](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scuderia_Ferrari). When Ferrari left Alfa Romeo, he went on to build his own cars. [Tazio Nuvolari](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tazio_Nuvolari) often drove for Alfa, winning many races before the [Second World War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_World_War).

In 1928, Nicola Romeo left, and in 1933 Alfa Romeo was rescued by the government, which then had effective control. Alfa Romeo became an instrument of Mussolini's Italy, a national emblem. During this period, it built bespoke vehicles for the wealthy, with bodies normally by [Carrozzeria Touring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carrozzeria_Touring) or [Pininfarina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pininfarina). This era peaked with the [Alfa Romeo 2900B Type 35](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfa_Romeo_8C) racers.

The Alfa factory (converted during wartime to the production of [Macchi C.202 Folgore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macchi_C.202_Folgore) engines: the Daimler-Benz 600 series built under license) was bombed during the Second World War and struggled to return to profitability after the war. The luxury vehicles were out. Smaller, mass-produced vehicles began to be produced beginning with the 1954 model year, with the introduction of the [Giulietta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfa_Romeo_Giulietta_(750/101)) series of *berline* (saloons/sedans), coupes and open two-seaters. All three varieties shared what would become the [Alfa Romeo overhead Twin Cam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfa_Romeo_Twin_Cam_engine) four-cylinder engine, initially displacing 1300 cc. This engine would eventually be enlarged to 2000 cc and would remain in production until 1995.

content.heading: Post-war
content: Once motorsports resumed after the Second World War, Alfa Romeo proved to be the car to beat in Grand Prix events. The introduction of the new formula ([Formula One](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Formula_One)) for single seat racing cars provided an ideal setting for Alfa Romeo's Tipo [158 Alfetta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfa_Romeo_158/159_Alfetta), adapted from a pre-war voiturette, and [Giuseppe Farina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giuseppe_Farina) won the first Formula One World Championship in 1950 in the 158. [Juan Manuel Fangio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juan_Manuel_Fangio) secured Alfa's second consecutive championship in 1951.

In 1952, Alfa Romeo experimented with its first front-wheel-drive compact car, "Project 13–61".[12] It had the same transverse-mounted, forward-motor layout as the modern front-wheel-drive automobile. Alfa Romeo made a second attempt in the late 1950s based on Project 13–61. It was to be called Tipo 103 and resembled the smaller version of its popular Alfa Romeo Giulia. However, due to the financial difficulties in post-war Italy, the Tipo 103 never saw production. Had Alfa Romeo produced it, it would have preceded the Mini as the first "modern" front-wheel-drive compact car. In the mid-1950s, Alfa Romeo entered into an agreement with [Brazil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brazil)'s Matarazzo Group to create a company called Fabral (*Fábrica Brasileira de Automóveis Alfa*, "the Brazilian Alfa automobile factory") to build the [Alfa Romeo 2000](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfa_Romeo_2000) there. After having received government approval, Matarazzo pulled out under pressure from Brazil's President [Juscelino Kubitschek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juscelino_Kubitschek) with the state-owned [FNM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fábrica_Nacional_de_Motores) company instead commenced building the car as the "FNM 2000" there in 1960.[13]

During the 1960s, Alfa Romeo concentrated on motorsports using production-based cars, including the [GTA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfa_Romeo_GTA) (standing for Gran Turismo Allegerita), an aluminium-bodied version of the [Bertone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gruppo_Bertone)-designed coupe with a powerful twin-plug engine. Among other victories, the GTA won the inaugural [Sports Car Club of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Car_Club_of_America)'s [Trans-Am](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trans-Am_Series) championship in 1966. In the 1970s, Alfa Romeo concentrated on prototype sports car racing with the [Tipo 33](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfa_Romeo_Tipo_33), with early victories in 1971. Eventually the Tipo 33TT12 gained the [World Championship for Makes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1975_World_Sportscar_Championship_season) for Alfa Romeo in 1975 and the Tipo 33SC12 won the [World Championship for Sports Cars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1977_World_Sportscar_Championship_season) in 1977.[14][15]

As Alfa Romeo was a state-controlled company, they were often subject to political pressure. To help industrialize Italy's [underdeveloped south](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_question), Alfa Romeo's new compact car was to be built at a new factory at [Pomigliano d'Arco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pomigliano_d'Arco) in [Campania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Campania). Even the car's name, *Alfa Sud* (Alfa South), reflected where it was built. 18 January 1968, saw a new company named "Industria Napoletana Costruzioni Autoveicoli Alfa Romeo-Alfasud S.p.A." being formed, 90% of which belonged to Alfa Romeo and 10% to Government controlled holding company [Finmeccanica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonardo_(company)).[16] This plant was built in the wake of France's [1968 protests](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/May_68) and Italy's [Hot Autumn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hot_Autumn) and was never "properly started."[17] The employees had mainly construction backgrounds and were not trained for factory work, while industrial relations were troublesome throughout. Absenteeism rates in the Pomigliano factory ran at 16.5 percent through the 1970s,[18] reaching as high as 28 percent.[19]

By the 1970s, Alfa Romeo was again in financial trouble, with the company running at about sixty percent of capacity in 1980.[17] Since Alfa Romeo was controlled by the Italian government owned Istituto per la Ricostruzione Industriale (IRI), a deal was made where about a quarter of worker's salaries were paid through state unemployment agencies to allow Alfa's plants to idle for two weeks every two months. An aging product lineup and very low productivity combined with near-permanent industrial unrest and Italy's high inflation rates kept Alfa Romeo firmly in the red.[17][20][19] Other creative measures were attempted to shore up Alfa, including an ultimately unsuccessful [joint venture with Nissan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfa_Romeo_Arna) endorsed by Alfa's then-president, Ettore Massacesi, and Prime Minister [Francesco Cossiga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francesco_Cossiga). By 1986, IRI was suffering heavy losses—with Alfa Romeo having not been profitable for the last 13 years[21]—and IRI president [Romano Prodi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romano_Prodi) put Alfa Romeo up for sale. Finmeccanica, the mechanical holdings arm of IRI and its predecessors owned Alfa Romeo since 1932. Prodi first approached fellow Italian manufacturer Fiat, which offered to start a joint venture with Alfa.

content.heading: Fiat takeover
content: Fiat withdrew its plan for a joint venture with Alfa Romeo when [Ford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ford_Motor_Company) put in an offer to acquire part of Alfa Romeo and restructure the company, while increasing its stake over time. However, Fiat chose to put in a bid to acquire the entirety of Alfa Romeo and offer job guarantees to Italian workers, an offer that Ford was unwilling to match. It also did not hurt any of the parties involved that an acquisition by Fiat would keep Alfa Romeo in Italian hands. In 1986, the deal was concluded with Alfa Romeo merged with traditional rival [Lancia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lancia) into Fiat's Alfa Lancia Industriale S.p.A.[21][20] Already in 1981, Alfa Romeo's then-President Ettore Massacesi had stated that Alfa would never use Fiat engines—the engines being, to a large extent, Alfa Romeo's identity—but would be happy to cooperate fully with everything else.[22]

Models produced from the 1990 onwards combined Alfa's traditional virtues of avant-garde styling and sporting panache with the economic benefits of product rationalisation, and include a "GTA" version of the [147](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfa_Romeo_147) hatchback, the [Giugiaro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giugiaro)-designed [Brera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfa_Romeo_Brera), and a high-performance exotic called the [8C Competizione](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfa_Romeo_8C_Competizione) (named after one of Alfa's most successful prewar sports and racing cars, the [8C](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfa_Romeo_8C) of the 1930s).

In 2005, [Maserati](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maserati) was bought back from [Ferrari](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferrari) and was now under Fiat's full control. The Fiat Group then created a sports and luxury division from Maserati and Alfa Romeo.[23] There is a planned strategic relationship between these two; engines, platforms and possibly dealers are shared.[24]

In the beginning of 2007, Fiat Auto S.p.A. was reorganized and four new automobile companies were created; Fiat Automobiles S.p.A., Alfa Romeo Automobiles S.p.A., Lancia Automobiles S.p.A. and Fiat Light Commercial Vehicles S.p.A. These companies were fully owned by Fiat Group Automobiles S.p.A. (from 2007 FCA Italy S.p.A.).[25]
On 24 June 2010, Alfa Romeo celebrated 100 years from its foundation.[26]

content.heading: Recent developments
content: Alfa Romeo has been suffering from falling sales. In 2010, it sold a total of about 112,000 units, which was significantly lower than Fiat CEO Marchionne's global sales target of 300,000. The company set about to achieve a sales target of 170,000 units in 2011, including 100,000 [Giulietta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfa_Romeo_Giulietta) and 60,000 [MiTo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfa_Romeo_Mito) models, but it actually sold 130,000 units that year.[30] Its medium-term target was 500,000 units by 2014 including 85,000 from the North American market.[31] In 2017 Alfa Romeo increased production by 62 percent, building a total of 150,722 vehicles at the company's three factories.[32]

On 16 January 2021, the operations of [Fiat Chrysler Automobiles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fiat_Chrysler_Automobiles) and [Groupe PSA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Groupe_PSA) were merged to form [Stellantis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stellantis) and the company was renamed Stellantis Italy.[33]

In spite of falling sales, Alfa Romeo CEO Jean-Philippe Imparato announced in 2021 that a new model would be launched every year between 2022 and 2026, starting with the much-delayed [Tonale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfa_Romeo_Tonale), with full electrification of new models from 2027.[34]

content.heading: Return to North America
content: Alfa Romeo was imported to the United States by [Max Hoffman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max_Hoffman) from the mid-1950s.[35] The Giulietta Spider was developed on the request of Max Hoffman, who proposed an open top version of the Giulietta.[36] In 1961 Alfa Romeo started exporting cars to the United States through its own dealer network.[37]
In 1995, Alfa Romeo ceased exporting cars to the United States,[38] the last model sold in that market being the 164 sedan.

On 5 May 2006, Alfa Romeo made its return to the US Market as announced by Fiat CEO [Sergio Marchionne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergio_Marchionne) after a series of rumours. North American sales resumed in October 2008, with the launch of the limited production 8C Competizione coupe with Alfa Romeo models being imported by Fiat's US subsidiary Chrysler.[39] Also in 2008, Alfa Romeo and Chrysler were reported to be in discussions over the possibility of producing Alfa Romeo cars in some Chrysler manufacturing plants that had shut down due to the company group's restructure and cost cutting. Instead, as reported by *The Wall Street Journal* in November 2009, Chrysler discontinued several Dodge and Jeep models while phasing in Alfa Romeo ones and the new Fiat 500.[40]

The next significant milestones in Alfa Romeo's North American return occurred in 2014, with the launch of the more affordable two-seater [4C coupe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfa_Romeo_4C). That year, Fiat Group Automobiles S.p.A. confirmed that its original agreement with Mazda Motor Corporation, for the speculated manufacturing of a new Alfa Romeo Spider based on the [Mazda MX-5](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mazda_MX-5) had been terminated mutually in December 2014. The proposed model for this joint venture became the [Fiat 124 Spider](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fiat_124_Spider_(2016)) convertible launched in 2015. In 2015, Alfa Romeo's return to this market was further bolstered by the automaker's display of the new [Giulia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfa_Romeo_Giulia_(952)) at the Los Angeles Auto Show. In February 2017, Chrysler featured its Alfa Romeo brand exclusively in three ads during [Super Bowl LI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_LI).[41]
Alfa Romeo's US importer, [FCA US LLC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chrysler), currently imports the Giulia, Stelvio, Tonale and 33 Stradale.

content.heading: Technological development
content: Alfa Romeo has introduced many technological innovations over the years, and the company has often been among the first users of new technologies. Its trademark [double overhead cam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Double_overhead_cam) engine was used for the first time in the 1914 [Grand Prix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfa_Romeo_Grand_Prix) car,[51] the first road car with such an engine, the [6C 1500 Sport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfa_Romeo_6C), appeared in 1928.

Alfa Romeo tested one of the first electronic fuel injection systems ([Caproni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caproni)-Fuscaldo) in the [Alfa Romeo 6C](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfa_Romeo_6C) 2500 with "Ala spessa" body in 1940 [Mille Miglia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mille_Miglia). The engine had six electrically operated injectors, fed by a semi-high pressure circulating fuel pump system.[52]

1969 models for the [North American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_America) market had [SPICA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SPICA) (Società Pompe Iniezione Cassani & Affini, a subsidiary of Alfa Romeo) [mechanical fuel injection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manifold_injection#Mechanical_controlling). According to Alfa Romeo, the engine's power output and performance were unchanged from the carburetted version. The SPICA system continued until the 1982 model year with the introduction of 2.0 liter [Bosch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Bosch_GmbH) [electronic fuel injection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fuel_injection#Multi-point_injection).

Mechanical [variable valve timing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variable_valve_timing) was introduced in the [Alfa Romeo Spider](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfa_Romeo_Spider), sold in the U.S. in 1980.[53] All Alfa Romeo Spider models from 1983 onward used electronic VVT.[54]

The 105 series [Giulia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfa_Romeo_Giulia) was quite an advanced car, using technologies such as all-wheel [disc brakes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disc_brake),[55] and a plastic radiator header tank. It had also the lowest [drag coefficient](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drag_coefficient) (Cd) in its class[56] The same trend continued with the Alfetta 2000 and GTV, which had quirks such as 50:50 [weight distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weight_distribution),[57][58] standard fit [alloy wheels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alloy_wheel) and [transaxle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transaxle).[59]

Newer innovations include complete [CAD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer-aided_design) design process used in designing the [Alfa Romeo 164](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfa_Romeo_164)[60] and an [automated/paddle-shift transmission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Automated_manual_transmission) called *[Selespeed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selespeed)* used in the [156](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfa_Romeo_156);[61] the 156 was also the world's first passenger car to use [Common rail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Common_rail) diesel engine.[62] The [Multiair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multiair) -an electro-hydraulic variable valve actuation technology used in [MiTo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfa_Romeo_MiTo) was introduced in 2009.[63] In 2016, the Alfa Romeo Giulia came with electrical brakes.[64]

content.heading: Body design
content: Many famous automotive design houses in Italy have accepted commissions to produce concepts and production vehicle shapes for Alfa Romeo. These include:

Construction techniques used by Alfa Romeo has been imitated by other carmakers, and in this way, the Alfa Romeo body designs have often been very influential. The following is a list of innovations, and where appropriate, examples of imitation by other car manufacturers:
1960s: Aerodynamics: The 116-series Giulia had a very low Cd. Toyota, in particular, sought to produce a similarly shaped series of vehicles at this time.

1970s: Fairing of bumpers: In order to meet American crash standards, Alfa Romeo formulated a design technique to incorporate bumpers into the overall bodywork design of vehicles so as to not ruin their design lines. The culmination of this design technique was the 1980s [Alfa Romeo 75](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfa_Romeo_75). The process was widely copied, particularly in Germany and Japan.

1980s: Design process: Model 164 manufacturing introduced complete CAD/CAM, with very little directly made by hand. Its influence is out of proportion to previous models. Its styling continues to influence today's models. Most manufacturers incorporated design ideas first expressed in the 164, including greater reliance on on-board computers.

1990s: Pseudo-coupé: Model 156 and 147, while four-door vehicles, represented themselves as two-doors with prominent front door handles, and less visible rear door-handle flaps. Honda used this style in its latest Civic hatchback, and a similar idea is also seen in the [Mazda RX-8](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mazda_RX-8) four-seat coupé and [Renault Clio V](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renault_Clio).

2000s: The Brera and 159: These vehicles' design, by Giorgetto Giugiaro, have proven influential in sedan and coupé styling, demonstrating that concept vehicles are often immediately translatable into road car form, providing that initial design takes place using CAD systems.

content.heading: Concept cars
content: Several concept cars have been made by Alfa Romeo:

The *[Berlina Aerodinamica Tecnica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfa_Romeo_BAT)* prototype cars were designed by Bertone as an exercise in determining whether streamlining and wind-tunnel driven designs would result in high performance on a standard chassis and whether the resulting vehicles would be palatable to the public. Alfa 1900 Sprint were the basis of the B.A.T. 5, 7 and 9.[65] The later B.A.T. 11 was based on the 8C Competizione.

The Tipo 33 racing car, with its high-revving 2000 cc V8 engine became the basis for a number of different concept cars during the 1960s and 1970s, two of which ultimately resulted in production vehicles. Most made their appearances at the Auto Salon Genève. Here is a brief list:
Gandini/Bertone Carabo (1968) – Marcello Gandini expressed ideas that would come to fruition in the Lamborghini Countach.
Tipo 33.2 (1969) – Designed by Pininfarina using a design already known from a Ferrari concept car.

Gandini/Bertone Montreal Concept (1967) – making its appearance at the 1967 Montreal Expo, this Giulia-based concept resulted in the production [Alfa Romeo Montreal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfa_Romeo_Montreal) road car with a variant of the Tipo 33's V8 engine.
Bertone/Giugiaro Navajo (1976) – A fully fibreglassed vehicle, and in some ways the epitome of Giugiaro's 'Origami' style of flat planes.

In general, concept cars for Alfa Romeo have generally become production vehicles, after some modification to make them suitable for manufacture, and to provide driver and passenger safety. The Zagato SZ, GTV, and Spider, Brera, and 159 are all good examples of Alfa Romeo's stylistic commitment in this direction.

content.heading: Original logo
content: Alfa Romeo's logo incorporates two [heraldic devices](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heraldry) traditionally associated with its birthplace, the city of [Milan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milan): A red cross, from the [emblem of Milan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flag_of_Milan), and the *[biscione](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biscione)*, a big [grass snake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grass_snake) and a child emerging from its mouth—emblem of the [House of Visconti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Visconti_of_Milan), rulers of the city in the 14th century.[66][67][68]
The logo was originally designed in 1910 by a young Italian [draughtsman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Technical_drawing) from the A.L.F.A. technical office, Romano Cattaneo.[69]

content.heading: Origin
content: In June 1910, the Società Anonima Darracq became Anonima Lombarda Fabbrica Automobili, and was readying its first model, the [24 HP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ALFA_24_HP). The board asked chief engineer [Giuseppe Merosi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giuseppe_Merosi) to devise a badge for the radiator shell of the new car; Merosi turned to his collaborators.[69] One of them, Cattaneo, was inspired by the [coat of arms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coat_of_arms) he had seen on the gates of [Castello Sforzesco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castello_Sforzesco) to include the *biscione* in the logo.[69] Merosi liked the idea, and together with Cattaneo came up with a sketch, then approved by managing director Ugo Stella; Cattaneo was entrusted with doing the final design.[69]

The original badge was round, of enamelled [brass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brass), measuring 65 mm (2.6 in) in diameter, and carried already all the present day accoutrements: the red cross on a white field of Milan on the left, a green *biscione* on a light blue field on the right, all surrounded by a blue ring inscribed with the words "ALFA" at the top and "MILANO" at the bottom.[70] In honour of the [King of Italy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Italy), the two words were separated by two [figure-eight knots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Figure-eight_knot)—named Savoy knots in Italian, and symbols of the then-reigning [House of Savoy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Savoy). Originally solid brass, the lettering was changed to white enamel in 1913.[71] In 1918, after the company had been bought by [Nicola Romeo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicola_Romeo), the wording "ALFA" was replaced with "ALFA-ROMEO".

In 1925, to commemorate the victory of the [Alfa Romeo P2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfa_Romeo_P2) in the inaugural [World Manufacturers' Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Manufacturers'_Championship) of [1925](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1925_Grand_Prix_season), a silver metal [laurel wreath](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurel_wreath) was added around the badge, used (in varying form) until 1982.[67][72] The addition of the wreath had enlarged the badge to 75 mm (3.0 in) diameter; in 1930 it was reduced back to 60 mm (2.4 in).[70]

content.heading: Post-war evolution
content: In 1946, after the [abolition of the monarchy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italian_constitutional_referendum,_1946) and proclamation of the [Italian Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italian_Republic), the figure-eight knots of the Savoy were replaced with two curvy lines.[73] Concurrently the badge was completely redesigned, and further reduced in size to 54 mm (2.1 in), a diameter unchanged ever since.[70] Made of stamped steel, the new badge bore the traditional elements—the scripts, the cross, a newly stylized *biscione* and a thin laurel wreath—embossed in antique silver, over a uniform [Alfa Red](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rosso_corsa) background, which had replaced the blue, white and light blue fields. This red-and-metal badge was used until 1950, when the company switched back to a traditionally enamelled and coloured one; in 1960 the badge was changed from brass to plastic, without substantial differences in design.[73]

At the beginning of the 1970s the all-new [Alfa Romeo Pomigliano d'Arco plant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfa_Romeo_Pomigliano_d'Arco_plant) (near [Naples](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naples)) was completed. When in 1972 the [Alfasud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfa_Romeo_Alfasud) produced there became the first Alfa Romeo passenger car manufactured outside Milan, the word "Milano", the curved lines and the hyphen between "Alfa" and "Romeo" were eliminated from the badge on all Alfa Romeos.[73] At the same time it was redesigned, most notably acquiring a modernised *biscione* and [typeface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Type_face).
After a mild restyling in 1982, which deleted the wreath and changed lettering and all chrome details to gold, this iteration of the badge remained in use until 2015.[74]

content.heading: 2015 redesign
content: On 24 June 2015, 105th anniversary of the company, a new logo was unveiled at a press event at the [Alfa Romeo Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfa_Romeo_Museum); together with the [Alfa Romeo Giulia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfa_Romeo_Giulia_(2015)) as part of the brand's relaunch plan.[75] The redesign was carried out by Robilant Associati, who had previously reworked several other [Fiat Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FCA_Italy) logos—including [Fiat Automobiles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fiat_Automobiles)' and [Lancia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lancia)'s.[76]

The logo colors have been reduced from four to three: the green of the *biscione*, the red of the cross, and the dark blue of the surrounding ring. Other changes are a new serif type face, and the absence of the split white and light blue fields, replaced by a single silver textured background.

content.heading: The Quadrifoglio logo
content: Since 1923, the *quadrifoglio* logo (also called the 'cloverleaf') has been the symbol of Alfa Romeo racing cars and since WWII, it has also been used to designate the higher trim models of the range. The *quadrifoglio* is usually placed on the side panels of the car, above or behind the front wheels—on the [front wings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fender_(vehicle)) in the case of modern vehicles. The logo consists of a green (or in some cases golden) [cloverleaf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clover) with four leaves, contained with a white triangle.

content.heading: History of the emblem
content: The *quadrifoglio* has been used on Alfa Romeo cars since the death of [Ugo Sivocci](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ugo_Sivocci) in 1923. As a friend of [Enzo Ferrari](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enzo_Ferrari), Sivocci was hired by Alfa Romeo in 1920 to drive in the four-man works team—[Alfa Corse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfa_Corse)—with [Antonio Ascari](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antonio_Ascari), Giuseppe Campari, and Enzo Ferrari. Sivocci was thought to have enormous experience, but often hampered by bad luck and considered the eternal second-placer. To banish his bad luck, when the [Targa Florio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Targa_Florio) came around, the driver painted a white square with a green four-leaf clover (the *quadrifoglio*) in the centre of the grille of his car. Sivocci had immediate success, crossing the finish line first. The *quadrifoglio* subsequently became the symbol of the racing Alfa Romeos with the victory at the Targa Florio. Almost as if to prove the magic effects of this symbol, Sivocci was killed while testing [Merosi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giuseppe_Merosi)'s new [P1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfa_Romeo_P1) at [Monza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monza), a few months after winning the Targa Florio. The [Salerno](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salerno) driver's P1, which went off the track on a bend, did not have the *quadrifoglio*. Since this period in 1923, the bodies of Alfa Romeo racing cars have been adorned with the *quadrifoglio* as a lucky charm. The white square was replaced with a triangle in memory of Ugo Sivocci.[77]

content.heading: Modern usage
content: The first road car to bear the *quadrifoglio* was the 1963 [Alfa Romeo Giulia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfa_Romeo_Giulia) TI Super, a variant of the Giulia saloon car devised for competition but put regularly on sale; it had green four-leaf clovers on its front wings, without the triangle. In the 1970s "Quadrifoglio Verde" or "Green Cloverleaf" became the trim level for each model's sportiest variant, equipped with the most powerful engine. The [Alfasud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfa_Romeo_Alfasud), [Sprint](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfa_Romeo_Sprint), [33](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfa_Romeo_33), [75](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfa_Romeo_75), [164](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfa_Romeo_164) and [145](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfa_Romeo_145_and_146) all had Quadrifoglio Verde versions. Also in the 1970s and through the 1980s golden four-leaf clover badges were used to denote the most luxurious and well-equipped variants of Alfa Romeo cars, named "Quadrifoglio Oro" or "Gold Cloverleaf". The [Alfasud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfa_Romeo_Alfasud), [Alfetta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfa_Romeo_Alfetta), [Alfa 6](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfa_Romeo_Alfa_6), [90](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfa_Romeo_90) and [33](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfa_Romeo_33) had Quadrifoglio Oro versions. In recent times the *quadrifoglio* was revived on the 2007 [Alfa Romeo 8C Competizione](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfa_Romeo_8C_Competizione) and Spider sports cars. With the [Alfa Romeo MiTo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfa_Romeo_MiTo) and [Giulietta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfa_Romeo_Giulietta_(940)), the Quadrifoglio Verde was reinstated as the sportiest trim level in the range, and green four-leaf clovers on the front wings are once again the hallmark of high-performance Alfa Romeos. Alfa Romeo's 2016 sport sedan, the all-new [Giulia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfa_Romeo_Giulia_(952)), was launched first in Quadrifoglio trim before the release of the base models.

sections.heading: Motorsport
content: Alfa Romeo has been involved with motor racing since 1911, when it entered two [24 HP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ALFA_24_HP) models in Targa Florio competition. Alfa Romeo won the first [World Manufacturers' Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Manufacturers'_Championship) in 1925 and the first [AIACR European Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AIACR_European_Championship) in 1931 and it scored wins at many races and motoring events such as [Targa Florio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Targa_Florio), [Mille Miglia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mille_Miglia) and [Le Mans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Le_Mans_24_Hours). Great success continued with [Formula One](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Formula_One), when Alfa Romeo won the first World [Formula One](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Formula_One) Championship in 1950 and won the second [Formula One](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Formula_One) Championship in 1951. The company also won international championships in [Prototypes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prototypes), Touring and Fast Touring categories in the 1960s and 1970s. Private drivers also entered some [rally](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rally_(sports)) competitions, with good results. Alfa Romeo has competed both as a constructor and an engine supplier, via works entries [Alfa Corse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfa_Corse), [Autodelta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autodelta) and private entries. Alfa Romeo's factory racing team was outsourced to Enzo Ferrari's [Scuderia Ferrari](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scuderia_Ferrari) between 1933 and 1938. Drivers included Tazio Nuvolari, who won the 1935 [German Grand Prix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_Grand_Prix) at the Nürburgring.

Alfa Romeo have been in a technical partnership with the [Sauber F1 Team](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sauber_F1_Team) since 2018.[78] In February 2019, Sauber announced that it would compete as [Alfa Romeo Racing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfa_Romeo_Racing) although the ownership, racing licence and management structure would remain unchanged.[79] Alfa Romeo ended their partnership with Sauber and left Formula One after the 2023 season.[80]

Alfa Romeo has won five [FIA European Formula 3 Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FIA_European_Formula_3_Championship) and five [FIA European Formula 3 Cups](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FIA_European_Formula_3_Cup) with the support from the Alfa Romeo stable Euroracing, who created the motor for the Formula 3 championship and with the support of Italian motor company Novamotor which work in the Formula 3 competition.

sections.heading: Production
content: In the 1960s, the main Alfa Romeo factory was moved from inside Milan to a very large and nearby area extending over the municipalities of [Arese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arese), [Lainate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lainate) and [Garbagnate Milanese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garbagnate_Milanese). However, since then the factory was moved to Arese, as the offices and the main entrance of the area were located there.

In the late 1960s, a number of European automobile manufacturers established facilities in South Africa to assemble right hand drive vehicles. [Fiat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fiat) and other Italian manufacturers established factories along with these other manufacturers, Alfa-Romeos were assembled in [Brits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brits,_North_West), outside [Pretoria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pretoria) in the [Transvaal Province](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transvaal_Province) of South Africa. With the imposition of sanctions by Western powers in the 1970s and 1980s, South Africa became self-sufficient, and in car production came to rely more and more on the products from local factories. This led to a set of circumstances where between 1972 and 1989, South Africa had the greatest number of Alfa Romeos on the road outside of Italy. The Alfa Romeos Brits plant was used from March 1983[81] until late 1985 to build [Daihatsu Charades](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daihatsu_Charade) for local consumption, but also for export to Italy in order to skirt Italian limits on Japanese imports.[82] For the last year the company was operating, the Daihatsu represented close to half of Alfa Romeo S.A. Ltd.'s total production.[83]

In late 1985, with the impending Fiat takeover and an [international boycott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disinvestment_from_South_Africa) of the South African [Apartheid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apartheid) government, Alfa Romeo withdrew from the market and closed the plant.

During the 1990s, Alfa Romeo moved car production to other districts in Italy. The [Pomigliano d’Arco plant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfa_Romeo_Pomigliano_d'Arco_Plant) produced the 155, followed by the 145 and the 146, while the [Arese plant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfa_Romeo_Arese_Plant) manufactured the SZ and RZ sports cars, the 164, the new Spider and the GTV. The 156 was launched in 1997 and in 1998 was voted "Car of the Year". The same year a new flagship, the 166 (assembled in Rivalta, near Turin) was launched. At the beginning of the third millennium, the 147 was released, which won the title of "[European Car of the Year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Car_of_the_Year) 2001". In 2003 the Arese factory was closed while only having some offices and the [Alfa Romeo Historical Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfa_Romeo_Museum).

content.heading: Current models
content: The [Alfa Romeo Giulia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfa_Romeo_Giulia_(2015)) was unveiled to the press at the Museo Storico Alfa Romeo in Arese, on 24 June 2015. This coincided with the company's 105th anniversary and saw the introduction of a revised logo. Sales were about 34,000 examples per year (2018), then fell to 20,000 per year (2019).

The [Alfa Romeo Stelvio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfa_Romeo_Stelvio) was unveiled at the 2016 [Los Angeles Auto Show](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_Auto_Show). The Stelvio is Alfa Romeo's first production SUV that competes in the same category as the [Porsche Macan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Porsche_Macan), [Jaguar F-Pace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaguar_F-Pace), [Audi Q5](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Audi_Q5), [Mercedes-Benz GLC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercedes-Benz_GLC-Class) and [BMW X3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BMW_X3). It is current top Alfa sales with less than 40,000 examples per year (2019).

The [Alfa Romeo Tonale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfa_Romeo_Tonale) is a compact crossover SUV (C-segment) introduced in March 2022 and the first new model introduced by the brand in six years and the first model introduced under the brand of Stellantis.

The [Alfa Romeo 33 Stradale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfa_Romeo_33_Stradale_(2023)) was unveiled on August 30, 2023, and is planned to be released in June 2024, with a limited production of 33 units. The car pays tribute to the [Alfa Romeo 33 Stradale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfa_Romeo_33_Stradale) of 1967.

The [Alfa Romeo Junior](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfa_Romeo_Junior_(2024)) (previously Milano) is a subcompact crossover SUV ([B-segment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B-segment)) introduced in April 2024. It is the brand's first B-segment SUV, and its first battery electric car.

content.heading: Carabinieri, Polizia, and the Italian government
content: In the 1960s, Alfa Romeo became famous for models specifically designed for [Italian police](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italian_State_Police) and [Carabinieri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carabinieri) (Italian national [gendarmerie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gendarmerie)); among them the "[Giulia Super](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfa_Romeo_Giulia#Giulia_TI_Super)" and the [2600 Sprint GT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfa_Romeo_2600). The colours of the Alfa Romeos used by the police ([Polizia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polizia_di_Stato)) were/are green/blue with white stripes and writing, known as "Pantera" (Panthers). The Carabinieri Alfa Romeros are dark blue with white roofs and red stripes, known as the "Gazzella" (Gazelles), a nickname meant to denote the speed and agility of these "Pattuglie" (patrol cars). However, the term "Pantera" came to be used interchangeably to refer to both agencies' vehicles, and helped create a public perception of the cars as no-nonsense, determined and respected.

Since then, Alfa Romeos remain the chosen vehicle of the [Carabinieri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carabinieri), Polizia Autostradale (highway police), [Guardia di Finanza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guardia_di_Finanza) (fiscal law enforcement) and the conventional police service ([Polizia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polizia_di_Stato)). The following Alfa Romeo cars have/can be found in service with the Italian police and/or government.[85]

Since the 1960s, the Italian Prime Minister has used Alfa Romeos (and lately the new [Maserati Quattroporte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maserati_Quattroporte)) as preferred government limousines. The 164 and 166 have found been particularly utilized in the last two decades.

content.heading: Trucks and light commercial vehicles
content: In 1930, Alfa Romeo presented a light truck in addition to heavy LCVs based on [Büssing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Büssing) constructions.[87] In the Second World War Alfa Romeo also built trucks for the Italian army ("35 tons anywhere") and later also for the German [Wehrmacht](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wehrmacht). After the war, commercial motor vehicle production was resumed.
In co-operation with [FIAT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FIAT) and [Saviem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saviem) starting from the 1960s different light truck models were developed.

The production of heavy LCVs in Italy was terminated in 1967. Heavy trucks continued to be built for a few years in [Brazil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brazil) by Alfa Romeo subsidiary [Fábrica Nacional de Motores](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fábrica_Nacional_de_Motores) under the name FNM. The last Alfa Romeo vans were the Alfa Romeo AR6 and AR8, rebadged versions of Iveco Daily and Fiat Ducato. The company also produced [trolleybuses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trolleybus) for many systems in Italy, Latin America,[88] Sweden,[89] Greece,[90] Germany, Turkey and South Africa. Later, Alfa Romeo concentrated only on passenger car manufacturing.

sections.heading: Other production
content: Although Alfa Romeo is best known as automobile manufacturer it has also produced commercial vehicles of various size, railway locomotives,[6] tractors, buses, trams, compressors, generators, an electric cooker,[93] marine and aircraft engines.

content.heading: Aircraft engines
content: An Alfa engine was first used on an aircraft in 1910 on the Santoni-Franchini biplane.[94] In 1932 Alfa Romeo built its first real aircraft engine, the D2 (240 bhp), fitted to [Caproni 101 D2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caproni_Ca.101). In the 1930s when Alfa Romeo engines were used for aircraft on a larger scale; the [Savoia Marchetti SM.74](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Savoia-Marchetti_S.74), [Savoia-Marchetti SM.75](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Savoia-Marchetti_SM.75), [Savoia-Marchetti SM.79](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Savoia-Marchetti_SM.79), [Savoia Marchetti SM.81](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Savoia-Marchetti_SM.81) and [Cant Z506B Airone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CANT_Z.506) all used Alfa Romeo manufactured engines.[95] In 1931, a competition was arranged where [Tazio Nuvolari](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tazio_Nuvolari) drove his [Alfa Romeo 8C](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfa_Romeo_8C) 3000 Monza against a [Caproni Ca.100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caproni_Ca.100) airplane.[96]

Alfa Romeo built various aircraft engines during the [Second World War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_World_War); the best known was the RA.1000 RC 41-I Monsone, a licensed version of the [Daimler-Benz DB 601](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daimler-Benz_DB_601). This engine made it possible to build efficient fighter aircraft like the [Macchi C.202 Folgore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macchi_C.202_Folgore) for the Italian army. After the Second World War Alfa Romeo produced engines for Fiat, [Aerfer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aerfer) and [Ambrosini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ambrosini_(aircraft_manufacturer)). In the 1960s Alfa Romeo mainly focused upgrading and maintaining [Curtiss-Wright](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curtiss-Wright), [Pratt & Whitney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pratt_&_Whitney), [Rolls-Royce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolls-Royce_Limited) and [General Electric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Electric) aircraft engines.

Alfa Romeo also built Italy's first [turbine engine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turboprop), installed to the [Beechcraft King Air](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beechcraft_King_Air). Alfa Romeo's Avio division was sold to [Aeritalia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aeritalia) in 1988,[97] from 1996 it was part of Fiat Avio.[98] Alfa Avio was also part of developing team to the new T700-T6E1 engine to the [NHI NH90](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NHI_NH90) helicopter.[99]

content.heading: Marine engines
content: Alfa Romeo also produced marine engines. The first marine engine was produced in 1929. Later, for three consecutive years: 1937-1938-1939 with remarkable affirmations, Alfa Romeo demonstrated its constructive efficiency by contributing to the development of marine engines.

sections.heading: Marketing and sponsorship
content: During the years Alfa Romeo has been marketed with different slogans like: "The family car that wins races" used in the 1950s in Alfa Romeo 1900 marketing campaign, "racing since 1911" used on most 1960s Alfa advertisements.[100] In the 1970s the Alfa Romeo 1750 GTV was marketed as "if this kind of handling is good enough for our racing cars, it's good enough for you."[101] The Giulia Sprint GTA was marketed as "The car you drive to work is a champion".[102] More recent slogans used are "Mediocrity is a sin", "Driven by Passion", "Cuore Sportivo", "Beauty is not enough" and present day "Without heart we would be mere machines". Also other more recent ones are: "It's not a car, it's an Alfa Romeo.", one of them after a couple argue in Italian.

As part of its marketing policy, Alfa Romeo sponsors a number of sporting events, such as the [Mille Miglia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mille_Miglia) rally.[103] It has sponsored the SBK [Superbike World Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Superbike_World_Championship) and [Ducati](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ducati) Corse since 2007, and the [Goodwood Festival of Speed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goodwood_Festival_of_Speed) for many years, and was one of the featured brands in 2010 when Alfa Romeo celebrated its 100th anniversary.[104][105] The [Alfa Romeo Giulietta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfa_Romeo_Giulietta_(2010)) has been used since Monza 2010 race as the safety car in Superbike World Championship events.[106] Alfa Romeo has been also shirt sponsor of [Eintracht Frankfurt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eintracht_Frankfurt) football club in period between 2013 and 2016.

In 2002, *[Alfa Romeo I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfa_Romeo_I)*, the first Alfa Romeo super [maxi yacht](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maxi_yacht) was launched. It finished first in at least 74 races including the 2002 [Sydney—Hobart Race](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydney_to_Hobart_Yacht_Race).[107] *Alfa Romeo II*, commissioned in 2005, measures 30 metres (98 ft) [LOA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Length_overall). It set a new elapsed-time record for monohulls in the 2009 Transpac race, of 5 days, 14 hours, 36 minutes, 20 seconds.[108] It finished first in at least 140 races. In mid-2008 *Alfa Romeo III* was launched for competitive fleet racing under the [IRC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IRC_(sailing)) rule. *Alfa Romeo III* measures 21.4 metres (70 ft) LOA and features interior design styled after the [Alfa Romeo 8C Competizione](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfa_Romeo_8C_Competizione).[109]

The [BBC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC) motoring show *[Top Gear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Top_Gear_(2002_TV_series))* repeatedly argued the significance of owning an Alfa Romeo car as a car enthusiast, stating that "You can't be a true petrolhead if you have never owned/or wanted to own an Alfa Romeo". Presenters [Jeremy Clarkson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Clarkson), [Richard Hammond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Hammond) and [James May](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_May) continuously praised Alfas for their beauty and driving characteristics even though Italian cars had a long-term bad reputation for unreliability. They argued that the owner build a personal relationship with the car despite all of its mechanical faults. Both Clarkson and May have previously owned Alfas (a [GTV6](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfa_Romeo_Alfetta) for Clarkson and an [Alfa 164](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfa_Romeo_164) for May) and both have stated that they regretted selling their Alfas the most.

As part of its U.S. relaunch, Alfa Romeo ran three [commercials](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_commercials) during [Super Bowl LI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_LI); the brand was the sole marque advertised by FCA during the game, after exclusively focusing on its [Jeep](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeep) brand at [Super Bowl 50](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_50).[41][110]

In February 2013, Alfa Romeo sponsored [University of St Andrews](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_St_Andrews) FS fashion show[111] which saw luxury fashion designer Luke Archer and milliner George Jenkins win with their Alfa Romeo inspired garments.

Alfa Romeo announced [Zhou Guanyu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zhou_Guanyu) as China's first Formula One racing driver for the 2022 season, hailed by both the team and the sport as a historic breakthrough in a key growth market.[112]
